Can you circumcise a buried penis?

At Beverley Clinic, we regularly circumcise babies, children, teenagers and adults with mild to severe buried penis. The penis needs to be properly assessed and brought forwards before circumcision so that its true length can be seen and the appropriate amount of foreskin can be removed.

Buried penis is particularly common in babies and young children, but it can also occur in older children, teenagers and adults.

There are different reasons why a penis may have a buried appearance. In some patients the penis itself is relatively small. In others, the penis is normal in size but the pubic area is relatively high or contains a prominent fatty pad, causing more of the penile shaft to sit within the surrounding tissue. Some patients have a combination of both factors.

Having a buried penis does not mean that you or your child cannot be circumcised at Beverley Clinic.

What is a buried penis?

A buried penis, sometimes called a hidden or concealed penis, is when part of the penis is hidden within the surrounding skin and pubic tissue, making the visible penis appear shorter than it actually is.

Buried penis is particularly common in babies and young children, but it can also occur in older children, teenagers and adults.

There are different reasons why a penis may have a buried appearance. In some patients the penis itself is relatively small. In others, the penis is normal in size but the pubic area is relatively high or contains a prominent fatty pad, causing more of the penile shaft to sit within the surrounding tissue. Some patients have a combination of both factors.

Having a buried penis does not mean that you or your child cannot be circumcised at Beverley Clinic.

We regularly circumcise patients with mild, moderate and severe buried penis, from babies through to adults. The important difference is that a buried penis needs to be recognised before circumcision and the procedure needs to be adapted to the individual's anatomy.

In particular, the practitioner needs to establish the true penile length and exactly how much skin can safely be removed.

Removing too much skin from a buried penis can create problems when the penis is fully extended. Removing too little may produce an unsatisfactory circumcision result. Experience in assessing this anatomy is therefore particularly important.

At Beverley Clinic, buried penis is something we routinely look for when examining patients before circumcision.

Why does a penis look buried?

There is no single reason.

The visible length of the penis depends not only on the size of the penis itself but also on its relationship with the surrounding pubic area.

A buried appearance may occur because:

  • The penis itself is relatively small
  • The pubic area is relatively high or prominent
  • There is a significant pubic fat pad surrounding the base of the penis
  • The penis naturally retracts into the surrounding tissue
  • There is a combination of these factors

This explains why two patients with a similar penile length can look very different externally.

A patient with a normal-sized penis but a relatively high or fatty pubic area may have much less of the shaft visible when standing or sitting normally.

When the surrounding tissue is gently compressed backwards, considerably more of the penis may become visible.

Is a buried penis the same as a small penis?

Not necessarily.

This is an important distinction.

Sometimes the penis itself is relatively small.

However, in many patients with a buried penis, the penis is normal in size but appears smaller because part of its length is hidden within the surrounding pubic tissue.

Some patients have elements of both.

During examination, gently compressing the tissue around the base of the penis and bringing the shaft forwards allows us to assess how much penile length is actually present.

For circumcision, this is considerably more useful than simply looking at how much penis is visible at rest.

Circumcision does not cause a buried penis

A buried penis is related to the relationship between the penis and the surrounding pubic tissue, rather than whether or not the foreskin is present.

If a child develops a prominent pubic fat pad that surrounds and conceals the penile shaft, the penis would have a buried appearance whether he had been circumcised or remained uncircumcised.

Circumcision can sometimes make the anatomy easier to recognise because the foreskin is no longer present.

In an uncircumcised boy with a buried penis, the foreskin may project beyond the underlying penile shaft. Parents may understandably look at the end of the foreskin and assume that the entire visible length represents the length of the penis itself.

However, foreskin extending beyond the glans should not be mistaken for penile shaft length.

When the pubic tissue at the base is pressed backwards and the penis is properly exposed, the relationship between the actual penile shaft and the surrounding pubic tissue becomes much clearer.

This is why a child who appears to have developed a buried penis after circumcision has not necessarily developed it because of the circumcision. The buried appearance can result from changes in growth, body proportions and the amount of tissue around the pubic area.

Can you circumcise a buried penis?

Yes. Having a buried penis does not prevent circumcision, but it does mean the procedure must be planned around the individual anatomy rather than treating it like a standard procedure.

Beverley Clinic Expertise

Buried penis circumcision at Beverley Clinic

We regularly circumcise patients with mild, moderate and severe buried penis, from babies through to adults. Before circumcision, we expose the true penile length and assess the amount of available skin so that the appropriate amount of foreskin can be removed. We also provide specific aftercare advice because a buried penis can retract into the surrounding pubic tissue during healing.

Related clinical conditions: Phimosis (tight foreskin) · BXO / lichen sclerosis · Re-circumcision & revision

Why is buried penis particularly important for circumcision?

Circumcision permanently removes foreskin.

With a buried penis, the practitioner cannot simply look at the amount of penis visible at rest and use that to decide how much skin to remove.

The penis needs to be fully brought forwards from the surrounding pubic tissue.

We then assess:

  • The true penile length
  • How much of the shaft is normally buried
  • The height and prominence of the pubic area
  • The amount of surrounding fatty tissue
  • How far the penis can be brought forwards
  • The amount and mobility of penile skin
  • The amount of foreskin that can safely be removed

This becomes increasingly important when the penis is significantly buried.

Our aim is to achieve an appropriate circumcision while retaining sufficient skin for the penis when it is fully extended.

Removing too much skin from a buried penis can create problems when the penis is fully extended, potentially causing painful tension or a skin deficiency. Conversely, removing too little skin may leave redundant foreskin and produce an unsatisfactory cosmetic outcome.

Circumcising mild and severe buried penis

At Beverley Clinic, we circumcise patients across the spectrum from mild to severe buried penis.

We do not regard the presence of a buried penis alone as a reason that circumcision cannot be performed.

Instead, we recognise that the circumcision requires experience and careful judgement.

The more buried the penis, the more important it becomes to understand what proportion of the penis is hidden and how much skin will be required when the penis is fully extended.

This is why identifying buried penis before beginning the circumcision is so important.

What happens after circumcision when the penis is buried?

A buried penis naturally tends to retract back into the surrounding pubic tissue.

This can happen immediately after circumcision or become more noticeable later as the child grows and body proportions change.

As the penis retracts, the shaft skin can move forwards towards the glans.

Parents may sometimes think that the foreskin is growing back or that the circumcision is being reversed. In reality, what they are seeing may simply be shaft skin moving forwards because the penis itself is sitting deeper within the surrounding pubic tissue.

The penis has not necessarily become shorter and the foreskin has not grown back.

This is why aftercare is particularly important for patients with a buried penis.

Buried penis circumcision aftercare

When the penis is buried within the surrounding pubic tissue, it naturally tends to retract inwards. As it does so, the shaft skin can move forwards towards the glans.

Following circumcision, it is important that the glans and the inner skin immediately behind it remain appropriately exposed during healing, according to the aftercare instructions provided by the clinic.

For babies and children, parents may therefore need to regularly expose the penis.

This is usually done by pressing down on the pubic area at the base of the penis to bring the penis forwards, while gently drawing the shaft skin backwards so that the glans and inner skin behind it can be seen.

For older children and adults with a buried penis, the same principle may form part of their own aftercare.

The purpose is not to stretch or pull forcefully. It is to prevent the penis from remaining continuously buried with the shaft skin sitting forwards against the glans during the healing period.

If the penis repeatedly retracts and the skin remains in contact with the glans, the surfaces can begin to stick together and penile adhesions may develop.

The amount and duration of this aftercare varies according to the patient's age, anatomy, degree of buried penis and stage of healing. We explain the appropriate technique following circumcision and provide follow-up support if parents or patients are unsure about the appearance.

For a ring circumcision, the timing of this care differs from a forceps-guided circumcision, so follow the instructions given specifically for the method used. See our circumcision aftercare page.

What if the penis becomes buried months or years after circumcision?

The same principle remains important even if the buried appearance develops well after the original circumcision.

If increasing pubic tissue causes the penis to sit further inwards, the shaft skin may move forwards and begin covering part of the glans.

Parents should not assume that the circumcision has somehow been reversed or that the foreskin has grown back.

What they are seeing may simply be shaft skin moving forwards because the penis itself is sitting deeper within the surrounding pubic tissue.

Where appropriate, regularly bringing the penis forwards by pressing down around its base and gently drawing the shaft skin backwards can help keep the glans exposed and reduce the tendency for the skin to stick.

If the skin has already become firmly attached, there is significant scarring, or parents are unsure whether the appearance is normal, they should contact us for assessment rather than forcibly trying to separate the skin themselves.

From our clinical experience

Buried penis is something we see very commonly, particularly in babies, but also in older children, teenagers and adults.

There are two features we particularly consider.

The first is the size and length of the penis itself.

The second is the relationship between the penis and the surrounding pubic area.

A patient can have a normal-sized penis but a relatively high or fatty pubic area that surrounds the base of the penis and hides a significant proportion of the shaft. Alternatively, the penis itself may be relatively small. Some patients have a combination of both.

When assessing a patient for circumcision, we therefore do not judge the penis simply by how much is visible at rest.

We compress the surrounding tissue and bring the penis forwards to understand its true anatomy.

This allows us to judge exactly how much skin should be removed during circumcision.

Afterwards, we also take into account the fact that the penis may naturally retract back into the surrounding tissue. This is particularly important when explaining aftercare and preventing the remaining skin from sticking to the glans during healing.

For us, the three important principles when circumcising a buried penis are:

Recognise the anatomy → expose the true penile length → remove the appropriate amount of skin.

Medical references

Our clinical guidance and information on buried and concealed penis are grounded in established paediatric surgical and urological standards, including:

  • NHS (National Health Service): Clinical guidance on childhood penile development, prepuce anatomy and post-circumcision care.
  • BAUS (British Association of Urological Surgeons): Clinical information on concealed / buried penis assessment and male foreskin surgery.
  • EAU (European Association of Urology): Paediatric urology guidelines on the management of the prepuce, concealed penis and foreskin conditions.
